title: How Blimps Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how blimps work, starting with the history of lighter-than-air craft: the Montgolfier hot air balloons, Henri Giffard's 1852 powered airship, and Zeppelin rigid airships. They cover the 1937 Hindenburg disaster at Lakehurst, New Jersey, its survivors, and the likely cause. They then describe the military use of blimps, Goodyear's blimp fleet, and the blimp anatomy: envelope, balloonets, suspension cables, gondola, control surfaces, and turbo-prop engines. They explain buoyancy and flight control, the helium shortage tied to the federal helium reserve, and the future of cargo airships. The episode closes with a listener mail story about a child of a heroin-addicted mother, responding to an earlier episode on sterilizing addicts.

segments.title: Opening banter and blimp terminology
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode and sort out the names for lighter-than-air craft: blimp, dirigible, Zeppelin, airship. Rigid, semi-rigid, and non-rigid are distinguished, and they briefly compare hot air balloons with steerable airships.

segments.title: Early history of airships
segments.summary: The Montgolfier brothers' hot air balloons and de Rozier's manned flight are covered. Henri Giffard's 1852 steam-powered, steerable airship is described, followed by Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin's rigid airships from 1900. The episode also covers the Led Zeppelin name.

segments.title: Commercial airship era and the Hindenburg flight
segments.summary: Airships carried passengers in the early twentieth century, with more than two thousand flights. The Hindenburg was a luxury airship and the pride of Nazi Germany. The hosts describe its May 1937 departure from Frankfurt, the Atlantic crossing, and arrival at Lakehurst, New Jersey, about twelve hours late.

segments.title: Hindenburg fire and survivors
segments.summary: The hosts describe the hydrogen-fueled fire during landing at Lakehurst, witness accounts of the flames, and survival by location in the ship. Of 97 people aboard, 62 survived. Two survivors are still alive. Testimony and early theories are covered.

segments.title: Likely cause of the Hindenburg disaster
segments.summary: A 2013 study is described that tested scale models and suggested static electricity from storm weather electrified the envelope. When ground crew grabbed the cables, a spark ignited a hydrogen leak. The hosts note that the fabric was not painted with a flammable coating.

segments.title: Military blimps and Goodyear's blimp fleet
segments.summary: After the Hindenburg, commercial airship travel declined. The US Navy used blimps as aerial carriers that could launch and retrieve light planes, and it had a planned landing-strip concept that was scrapped. Goodyear built a blimp fleet that became known for aerial sports coverage and appeared in the film Black Sunday.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A sponsor break separates the history from the explanation of how blimps work.

segments.title: Blimp anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts go through the parts of a blimp: the envelope made of neoprene and polyester with helium, low internal pressure, nose cone battens, mooring hook, balloonets for trim, suspension cables, and the gondola. They also describe the rudders, elevators, boost tab, and the wheel and pedal controls.

segments.title: Engines, fuel, maintenance, and flight
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the turbo-prop engines, air scoops that use prop wash to fill the balloonets, speeds, fuel use, and avgas. They explain buoyancy: helium's lift, positive and neutral buoyancy, and how filling or emptying the balloonets controls ascent and descent. Ground crew support and weather limits are also covered.

segments.title: Helium shortage and the future of airships
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the federal helium reserve in Texas, its sale by the Bureau of Land Management, and resulting shortages. They then cover the future of airships, including military and cargo designs such as the Lockheed Martin P-791 and the Dragon Dream. They describe the Dragon Dream hangar collapse and the scrapped Department of Defense program.
